claim: Capcom introduced the CP System in 1988; Forgotten Worlds was its first game.
evidence: The Games Machine issue 19, June 1989, 'Capcom: a captive audience' (Robin Hogg and Dominic Handy), p.24; Forgotten Worlds review p.30
Fabien Sanglard, The Book of CP-System (self-published, May 2026 build; modern book)
MAME source, src/mame/capcom/cps1.cpp, cps1.h and cps1_v.cpp (Paul Leaman and MAME contributors)
qualification: Checked. TGM: 'their first super system release, Forgotten Worlds (touring the arcade circuit some eight months ago)'. The p.30 review: 'the first of Capcom's games to use the awesome new generation CP graphics chip'. MAME lists Forgotten Worlds as a 1988 game. Retro Gamer 42 (2007) also says the system 'debuted in 1988 with ... Forgotten Worlds'.

claim: Capcom's publicity put the development at two to two-and-a-half years and millions: £5.5 million in The Games Machine, and two years and five million dollars from a Forgotten Worlds flyer that Sanglard calls questionable. ACE said Capcom 'threw millions of dollars' at it.
evidence: The Games Machine issue 19, June 1989, 'Capcom: a captive audience' (Robin Hogg and Dominic Handy), p.24; Forgotten Worlds review p.30
Fabien Sanglard, The Book of CP-System (self-published, May 2026 build; modern book)
ACE (Advanced Computer Entertainment) issue 26, November 1989, coin-op column, p.22
qualification: Checked: TGM says 'two-and-a-half years development' and 'costing £5.5 million to develop'. Sanglard p.37 and note [5] on p.235 say the figure comes from a flyer that 'also mentioned three Motorola 68000s'. Present it as Capcom's claim.

claim: Capcom staked the company on the board: TGM wrote that Capcom had 'practically staked their company on the new super chips', and Okamoto told Gamest 'we have gambled everything on it'.
evidence: The Games Machine issue 19, June 1989, 'Capcom: a captive audience' (Robin Hogg and Dominic Handy), p.24; Forgotten Worlds review p.30
Fabien Sanglard, The Book of CP-System (self-published, May 2026 build; modern book)
qualification: The Okamoto wording reaches us only through Sanglard's quotation (p.37, note [26]: Gamest #38, 1989-10-01). Nothing shows that Sanglard translated it himself, so the entry now says he 'quotes' it. The stake itself is corroborated by TGM.

claim: Sanglard gives the board's aims as lower production cost through one standard machine, cheaper game boards of mostly ROMs sold separately, stable development tools, graphics to match Sega and Namco, and protection from bootleggers who had copied Capcom's off-the-shelf boards. The CP System was designed so that one machine would stay in the cabinet while games changed.
evidence: Fabien Sanglard, The Book of CP-System (self-published, May 2026 build; modern book)
The Games Machine issue 19, June 1989, 'Capcom: a captive audience' (Robin Hogg and Dominic Handy), p.24; Forgotten Worlds review p.30
ACE (Advanced Computer Entertainment) issue 26, November 1989, coin-op column, p.22
Wireframe issue 54, August 2021, 'System Profile: CP System', pp.80-85
qualification: Sanglard pp.37-38 and TGM ('easier for your local arcade owner to swap games in cabinets') state it as an aim. ACE says swapping worked 'in theory'. Retro Gamer 42 (2007) says the CPS-1 base and game boards were 'sold in its entirety for each arcade title', so the lede now states it as the design intention, not as practice.

claim: An estimated 200,000 bootleg Capcom boards circulated in Mexico.
evidence: Fabien Sanglard, The Book of CP-System (self-published, May 2026 build; modern book)
qualification: Sanglard p.38, note [45]: Matt Leone, 'Street Fighter 2: Oral History', 2014-02-03. Leone was not read directly. The entry attributes the figure.

claim: The board was three stacked PCBs handled as one unit: A (processors, sound, CPS-A and video memory, the same for every game), B (the game's socketed ROMs plus per-game PALs that build the memory map), and C (the CPS-B, where most of the protection lived, revised far more often).
evidence: Fabien Sanglard, The Book of CP-System (self-published, May 2026 build; modern book)
ACE (Advanced Computer Entertainment) issue 26, November 1989, coin-op column, p.22
MAME source, src/mame/capcom/cps1.cpp, cps1.h and cps1_v.cpp (Paul Leaman and MAME contributors)
qualification: Checked against Sanglard pp.40-47 and ACE's 'interlocking mother boards'. The role split in detail is Sanglard's.

claim: The CP System used one Motorola 68000 at 10 MHz (12 MHz on later games) and a Z80 at 3.58 MHz driving a Yamaha YM2151 FM chip and an OKI MSM6295 for sampled sound.
evidence: MAME source, src/mame/capcom/cps1.cpp, cps1.h and cps1_v.cpp (Paul Leaman and MAME contributors)
Fabien Sanglard, The Book of CP-System (self-published, May 2026 build; modern book)
qualification: Checked: MAME XTAL(10'000'000) 'verified on pcb', 12 MHz on later sets, Z80 and YM2151 at 3.579545 MHz. Sanglard pp.41 and 50 agree.

claim: The period press got the processor count wrong: ACE in 1989 reported 'two 68000's', a claim repeated in Italy's K, and a Forgotten Worlds flyer claimed three.
evidence: ACE (Advanced Computer Entertainment) issue 26, November 1989, coin-op column, p.22
K (Italy) issue 12, December 1989, coin-op column, pp.27-28
Fabien Sanglard, The Book of CP-System (self-published, May 2026 build; modern book)
qualification: Checked: ACE says 'the CP has got 2 68000's chugging away inside'. K's masthead says it is published 'su licenza della EMAP B&CP' ('il CP ha dentro due velocissimi 68000'), so ACE and K count as one source. The three-68000 flyer is known only through Sanglard's note [5].

claim: Two custom chips, CPS-A and CPS-B, did the graphics. Sanglard says Ricoh made them exclusively for Capcom, with metal grids layered on top to deter decapping.
evidence: Fabien Sanglard, The Book of CP-System (self-published, May 2026 build; modern book)
ACE (Advanced Computer Entertainment) issue 26, November 1989, coin-op column, p.22
qualification: ACE corroborates 'two custom-designed, very highly integrated chips' and 'reluctant to reveal more'. The Ricoh fabrication and the metal grids are single-sourced to Sanglard (p.120, citing Eduardo Cruz [32]).

claim: The usable picture was 384 x 224 pixels at about 59.6 Hz (an 8 MHz dot clock with 512 x 262 total), wider than the Mega Drive's or Neo Geo's 320 and the Super NES's 256.
evidence: Fabien Sanglard, The Book of CP-System (self-published, May 2026 build; modern book)
MAME source, src/mame/capcom/cps1.cpp, cps1.h and cps1_v.cpp (Paul Leaman and MAME contributors)
qualification: Checked: MAME cps1.h gives a 16 MHz/2 pixel clock, HTOTAL 512 with visible 64-448, and VTOTAL 262 with visible 16-240. Sanglard pp.72-73 gives 59.6374 Hz. The comparison with other machines is Sanglard's.

claim: Graphics came from three scrolling tile layers (8x8, 16x16 and 32x32 tiles), a sprite layer and two hardware starfield layers. Only Forgotten Worlds and Strider used the starfields for stars; Ghouls 'n Ghosts put its dark sky on one.
evidence: Fabien Sanglard, The Book of CP-System (self-published, May 2026 build; modern book)
MAME source, src/mame/capcom/cps1.cpp, cps1.h and cps1_v.cpp (Paul Leaman and MAME contributors)
qualification: Checked: MAME cps1_v.cpp says 'Only Forgotten Worlds and Strider use the starfield'. Sanglard pp.89-91 and 96 cover the layers, the Ghouls sky on STAR1 and the Hyper Fighting black background.

claim: The sprite hardware could draw at most 256 sprite tiles per frame.
evidence: Fabien Sanglard, The Book of CP-System (self-published, May 2026 build; modern book)
qualification: Sanglard p.106.

claim: Colours were 16-bit: 4 bits each of red, green and blue plus 4 bits of brightness, giving 65,536 possible colours, held in 16-colour palettes with 32 palettes per layer.
evidence: Fabien Sanglard, The Book of CP-System (self-published, May 2026 build; modern book)
qualification: Sanglard pp.79 and 82.

claim: Each game's B-board carried 2-8 MiB of graphics ROM out of a 12 MiB maximum, because ROM was expensive. Final Fight had 2 MiB, the Street Fighter II games 6 MiB and Dynasty Wars 8 MiB.
evidence: Fabien Sanglard, The Book of CP-System (self-published, May 2026 build; modern book)
qualification: Sanglard p.45. His prose says only Dynasty Wars got 8 MiB, but his p.33 table also gives Mega Man: The Power Battle 8 MiB, so 'the most of any' was removed.

claim: About thirty games appeared on the board between 1988 and 1995, from Forgotten Worlds to Mega Man: The Power Battle, including Ghouls 'n Ghosts, Strider, U.N. Squadron, Final Fight, Street Fighter II and its updates, Captain Commando and Knights of the Round.
evidence: Fabien Sanglard, The Book of CP-System (self-published, May 2026 build; modern book)
Retro: The Ultimate Retro Companion volume 2 (Imagine Publishing; a compilation from gamesTM's retro section, undated), Capcom feature, pp.138-140
MAME source, src/mame/capcom/cps1.cpp, cps1.h and cps1_v.cpp (Paul Leaman and MAME contributors)
qualification: Sanglard says 'more than thirty' (pp.32 and 125), and his tables list 28 CPS-1 and 5 Dash games. The companion book says 'home to 29 titles', but it is a gamesTM compilation ('Retro, Volume 2: The Ultimate Retro Companion from gamesTM', undated), not Retro Gamer, and the entry now names it correctly. MAME credits Pang! 3 to Mitchell.

claim: Sources disagree on the second game: The Games Machine called Strider Capcom's second 'super chip' release, while Sanglard's games table lists Ghouls 'n Ghosts second and its ROMs carry the date 26 October 1988.
evidence: The Games Machine issue 19, June 1989, 'Capcom: a captive audience' (Robin Hogg and Dominic Handy), p.24; Forgotten Worlds review p.30
Fabien Sanglard, The Book of CP-System (self-published, May 2026 build; modern book)
MAME source, src/mame/capcom/cps1.cpp, cps1.h and cps1_v.cpp (Paul Leaman and MAME contributors)
qualification: The companion book was removed as support, because it does not put Ghouls second. Retro Gamer 29 (2006), which the reviewed ghouls-n-ghosts entry cites, does call it 'the sophomore CPS1 release', but this entry does not cite that issue. Sanglard's own prose (p.29) pairs 'Forgotten Worlds and Strider' as the first glimpse. This entry agrees with the reviewed ghouls-n-ghosts entry ('second'). The reviewed strider and arcade-hardware entries put Strider straight after Forgotten Worlds.

claim: Contemporary reaction was mixed: ACE thought the games technically outstanding but, apart from Strider, unoriginal, and C+VG found UN Squadron and 'virtually every other CP System game' unexciting at a 1989 show.
evidence: ACE (Advanced Computer Entertainment) issue 26, November 1989, coin-op column, p.22
Computer and Video Games issue 96, November 1989, trade-show report
qualification: Checked verbatim. The C+VG show was the AMOA show.

claim: Capcom's protection relied on the CPS-B, which changed from game to game (about 25 versions, with register layouts that moved) and blanked the screen when it detected wrong writes.
evidence: Fabien Sanglard, The Book of CP-System (self-published, May 2026 build; modern book)
MAME source, src/mame/capcom/cps1.cpp, cps1.h and cps1_v.cpp (Paul Leaman and MAME contributors)
qualification: Sanglard pp.121-123. His figure of twenty-five is itself cited to MAME's video driver [15]. The blanking behaviour is Sanglard's, citing Loïc Petit [29].

claim: From Three Wonders (1991), every board used the CPS-B-21, which kept its per-game configuration in battery-backed RAM and multiplied numbers for the game to check. A flat battery left the board dead (the 'suicide battery'). Hobbyists revive boards by patching the game ('phoenixing') or by rewriting the configuration ('de-suiciding').
evidence: Fabien Sanglard, The Book of CP-System (self-published, May 2026 build; modern book)
MAME source, src/mame/capcom/cps1.cpp, cps1.h and cps1_v.cpp (Paul Leaman and MAME contributors)
qualification: Checked: Sanglard pp.121-125. MAME says 'from here onwards the CPS-B board has suicide battery and multiply protection' and mentions desuicided boards.

claim: Sanglard quotes Capcom's chief executive Kenzo Tsujimoto calling the CP System 'the only PCB hardware today that cannot be copied', footnoted to the Gamest #38 Okamoto interview.
evidence: Fabien Sanglard, The Book of CP-System (self-published, May 2026 build; modern book)
qualification: Sanglard p.119 attributes it to 'Kenzo Tsujimoto, Capcom CEO [26]', and note [26] is 'Yoshiki Okamoto interview' (Gamest #38). The attribution conflict is now stated in the prose.

claim: The protection did not stop the bootleggers. Pirated and modified Street Fighter II boards (the 'Rainbow' editions among them) spread, and Hyper Fighting in 1992 was partly Capcom's answer to pirate copies.
evidence: Wireframe issue 54, August 2021, 'System Profile: CP System', pp.80-85
Edge issue 133, February 2004, Street Fighter series feature
MAME source, src/mame/capcom/cps1.cpp, cps1.h and cps1_v.cpp (Paul Leaman and MAME contributors)
qualification: Checked: Wireframe asks 'who doesn't remember Street Fighter II: Rainbow Edition at their local leisure centre?'. Edge 133's Hyper Fighting entry: 'one final outing on the aging CPS1 board in an attempt to counter the ever-increasing number of pirate copies'. MAME has the Rainbow and Red Wave sets.

claim: Replica CPS-A and CPS-B chips were made under the name COMCO.
evidence: Fabien Sanglard, The Book of CP-System (self-published, May 2026 build; modern book)
qualification: Sanglard p.126, citing Eduardo Cruz [30].

claim: The CP System Dash (CPS-1.5) of 1992-93 boxed the board in grey plastic and added a QSound board and an encrypting 'Kabuki' Z80 whose key needed a second battery. Five games used it, among them Cadillacs and Dinosaurs and Warriors of Fate.
evidence: Fabien Sanglard, The Book of CP-System (self-published, May 2026 build; modern book)
Wireframe issue 54, August 2021, 'System Profile: CP System', pp.80-85
MAME source, src/mame/capcom/cps1.cpp, cps1.h and cps1_v.cpp (Paul Leaman and MAME contributors)
qualification: 'Beginning with' changed to 'among them': MAME dates Warriors of Fate 921031 and Cadillacs and Dinosaurs 930201, while Sanglard puts both in 1992. 'Same hardware' changed to 'the CP System', since MAME says the Q-Sound A-board drops the Z80 and the OKI.

claim: CPS II, launched with Super Street Fighter II in 1993, followed the board, encrypted the game program, and was not fully reverse-engineered until 2007.
evidence: Edge issue 7, April 1994, ATEI show report
Fabien Sanglard, The Book of CP-System (self-published, May 2026 build; modern book)
Wireframe issue 54, August 2021, 'System Profile: CP System', pp.80-85
qualification: 'Replaced' changed to 'followed', because CPS-1 games continued to 1995. Sanglard p.129 independently gives 2007 for the full reverse-engineering.

claim: Capcom developed for the board using Sharp X68000 computers; Akiman said in 2018 that the CAT-1 SDK began during Street Fighter II and ran on the X68000. Capcom also ported several CPS-1 games to the X68000 itself.
evidence: Fabien Sanglard, The Book of CP-System (self-published, May 2026 build; modern book)
qualification: Sanglard pp.38, 205 and 211-212. His text says 'CAT-1', but his bibliography [59] titles Akiman's post 'The CPS-1 SDK, a.k.a CAT-A'. Note [60] is Takenori Kimoto, not Akiman. Sanglard also says developers 'never detailed to what extent SHARP's machine was involved'.

claim: Wireframe dates Capcom's home unit, the CPS Changer ('a home console version of the CPS hardware'), to 1994; in March 1995 SuperGamePower reported a Capcom adapter it called the 'CPS II Changer' that ran arcade boards on a TV, sold with a 'SSF Turbo' board for US$330.
evidence: Wireframe issue 54, August 2021, 'System Profile: CP System', pp.80-85
SuperGamePower (Brazil) year 1 issue 12, March 1995, news page
qualification: Now attributed to each source separately. Super Street Fighter II Turbo is a CPS-2 game (Sanglard's CPS-2 table, p.128), so the magazine's 'CPS II' naming may not be a mistake. Whether its item is the same product as Wireframe's CPS Changer is unconfirmed. The 1994 date rests on Wireframe alone.

claim: By early 1998 the Callus emulator ran nearly all CPS-1 games on PCs, as reported in Italy's The Games Machine and Brazil's SuperGamePower.
evidence: The Games Machine (Italy) issue 105, February 1998, emulation news
SuperGamePower (Brazil) year 5 issue 59, February 1999, emulator guide
qualification: Checked verbatim. TGM Italy issue 103 (December 1997), cited in the Sources list, reported Callus emulating CPS-1 even earlier.

claim: The name expands to 'Capcom Play System'.
evidence: Retro: The Ultimate Retro Companion volume 2 (Imagine Publishing; a compilation from gamesTM's retro section, undated), Capcom feature, pp.138-140
qualification: Attributed in the prose and set against Sanglard's 'nothing ever officially transpired except for a code name, CP-System'. The source is gamesTM's 'Retro Volume 2: The Ultimate Retro Companion', undated, not Retro Gamer. Retro Gamer 29 (2006) and 42 (2007) also expand it, but they come from the same publisher and are not independent of it, and none is a Capcom source.

claim: The Magnavox Odyssey (model 1TL200), launched in 1972, was the first home video game console.
evidence: Ralph H. Baer, Videogames: In the Beginning (Rolenta Press, 2005)
Marty Goldberg, 'Retroinspection: Magnavox Odyssey', in Retro Gamer, Videogames Hardware Handbook volume 1, 2nd edition (Imagine Publishing, 2016), pp. 8–15
Electronic Games, vol. 1 no. 2, March 1982, p. 8 (feature on Odyssey² designers)
Steve Bloom, interview with Ralph Baer, Video Games, vol. 1 no. 5, February 1983, pp. 20–24 and 80–81
Computer History Museum, 'Odyssey Game Console', catalogue no. 102752091, https://www.computerhistory.org/collections/catalog/102752091
qualification: Checked. Electronic Games (p. 8) calls it 'the very first videogame system' and 'The very first home videogame'; Retro Gamer calls it 'the very first commercial videogame console'. Agrees with reviewed people/ralph-baer and games/pong. Baer and the CHM record give model 1TL200.

claim: Sanders, a defence electronics company, demonstrated the Brown Box to television makers and signed a preliminary agreement with Magnavox in January 1971, handing over the prototype and its design data to Magnavox engineers in Fort Wayne. The Odyssey's circuitry was almost identical to the Brown Box's ('not much different', in Baer's words).
evidence: Ralph H. Baer, Videogames: In the Beginning (Rolenta Press, 2005)
Marty Goldberg, 'Retroinspection: Magnavox Odyssey', in Retro Gamer, Videogames Hardware Handbook volume 1, 2nd edition (Imagine Publishing, 2016), pp. 8–15
qualification: Baer calls the January 1971 agreement 'preliminary'; Retro Gamer calls it a licensing agreement. Both quotes ('not much different', 'basically copied all our sub-circuitry except ... color') checked in Baer, pp. 58–59 and 73.

claim: During development Magnavox called it Skill-O-Vision and tested it on the public in July 1971 (San Diego) and October 1971 (Grand Rapids, Michigan), with questionnaires asking about cards versus switches. The response led Magnavox to plan a May 1972 introduction, and the product took the Odyssey name in early 1972.
evidence: Ralph H. Baer, Videogames: In the Beginning (Rolenta Press, 2005)
Marty Goldberg, 'Retroinspection: Magnavox Odyssey', in Retro Gamer, Videogames Hardware Handbook volume 1, 2nd edition (Imagine Publishing, 2016), pp. 8–15
qualification: Baer's 'Will The Consumer Like Skill-O-Vision?' section names San Diego (July) and Grand Rapids (October) at Magnavox Home Entertainment Centers, which corrects the earlier note that Baer says only 'California'. A different passage of the book (p. 73) says only 'California'.

claim: To save money Magnavox dropped the Brown Box's colour circuitry and replaced its sixteen game-selection switches with plug-in printed-circuit cards, which Baer called 'a stroke of genius'.
evidence: Ralph H. Baer, Videogames: In the Beginning (Rolenta Press, 2005)
Marty Goldberg, 'Retroinspection: Magnavox Odyssey', in Retro Gamer, Videogames Hardware Handbook volume 1, 2nd edition (Imagine Publishing, 2016), pp. 8–15
qualification: Checked. Retro Gamer gives the chroma saving as $1.64, which matches the Fritsche memo Baer reproduces.

claim: The cards held no program. They rewired circuits already in the console for each game, and Baer called this 'the elementary forerunner of ROM'.
evidence: Steve Bloom, interview with Ralph Baer, Video Games, vol. 1 no. 5, February 1983, pp. 20–24 and 80–81
Marty Goldberg, 'Retroinspection: Magnavox Odyssey', in Retro Gamer, Videogames Hardware Handbook volume 1, 2nd edition (Imagine Publishing, 2016), pp. 8–15
qualification: Quote checked on p. 80 and attributed to Baer in the entry.

claim: The console used discrete parts with no integrated circuits: in Baer's words 'basically 40 transistors and a pile of diodes', because ICs 'back then were so damn expensive'. They sat on a motherboard with plug-in 'baby' boards. Baer told Retro Gamer the circuitry was 'nearly all digital and pulse circuitry'.
evidence: Steve Bloom, interview with Ralph Baer, Video Games, vol. 1 no. 5, February 1983, pp. 20–24 and 80–81
Ralph H. Baer, Videogames: In the Beginning (Rolenta Press, 2005)
Marty Goldberg, 'Retroinspection: Magnavox Odyssey', in Retro Gamer, Videogames Hardware Handbook volume 1, 2nd edition (Imagine Publishing, 2016), pp. 8–15
qualification: All three accounts are Baer's, so the entry attributes them to him. The phrase 'in 1971' was removed because the interview says 'back then'.

claim: The console could draw only a few square spots and a dividing line, with no on-screen score and no sound. Baer said nothing more complex than a net line, paddles and balls was possible; overlays were used because complex backgrounds were 'out of the question pricewise', and 'scoring was also too damn expensive'.
evidence: Steve Bloom, interview with Ralph Baer, Video Games, vol. 1 no. 5, February 1983, pp. 20–24 and 80–81
Ralph H. Baer, Videogames: In the Beginning (Rolenta Press, 2005)
Marty Goldberg, 'Retroinspection: Magnavox Odyssey', in Retro Gamer, Videogames Hardware Handbook volume 1, 2nd edition (Imagine Publishing, 2016), pp. 8–15
qualification: The quote splice was corrected. 'No sound' rests on Bushnell's hedged court testimony in Baer's book ('I don't think it had any sound effects') and Baer's account of Alcorn adding sound to Pong. Lovece (Video Games, Jan 1984, p. 42) says Pong 'sounded like the Odyssey game', which conflicts with this; see concerns.

claim: The console ran on six C cells giving 9 volts, and an AC adaptor was sold separately.
evidence: Ralph H. Baer, Videogames: In the Beginning (Rolenta Press, 2005)
Marty Goldberg, 'Retroinspection: Magnavox Odyssey', in Retro Gamer, Videogames Hardware Handbook volume 1, 2nd edition (Imagine Publishing, 2016), pp. 8–15
David Winter, 'Magnavox Odyssey', PONG-Story, https://pong-story.com/odyssey.htm
qualification: Baer (p. 73) and Retro Gamer say C cells; Winter says six Eveready batteries and lists the AC adaptor as an extra purchase. The CHM record says D cells, and the entry's Sources section records that disagreement.

claim: Two wired controllers each had horizontal, vertical and 'English' knobs; the console had speed and centre-line knobs.
evidence: Marty Goldberg, 'Retroinspection: Magnavox Odyssey', in Retro Gamer, Videogames Hardware Handbook volume 1, 2nd edition (Imagine Publishing, 2016), pp. 8–15
Ralph H. Baer, Videogames: In the Beginning (Rolenta Press, 2005)
Computer History Museum, 'Odyssey Game Console', catalogue no. 102752091, https://www.computerhistory.org/collections/catalog/102752091
qualification: Agrees with reviewed hardware/paddle-controller.

claim: Magnavox's engineers added a Game/TV switch box to meet FCC limits on r.f. leakage. Baer wrote that millions of similar boxes were copied by makers 'all across the globe'.
evidence: Ralph H. Baer, Videogames: In the Beginning (Rolenta Press, 2005)
David Winter, 'Magnavox Odyssey', PONG-Story, https://pong-story.com/odyssey.htm
qualification: Winter's background text repeats Baer's account almost word for word, so the two are not independent. The copying claim is attributed to Baer.

claim: It sold for $100 ($99.95) with six cards playing twelve games with overlays, plus playing cards, dice, play money and other pieces; the rifle cost $25 more.
evidence: Ralph H. Baer, Videogames: In the Beginning (Rolenta Press, 2005)
David Winter, 'Magnavox Odyssey', PONG-Story, https://pong-story.com/odyssey.htm
qualification: Baer gives $100 and Winter $99.95. A 1972 newspaper clipping reproduced in Baer's book wrongly says '12 printed-circuit game program cards'.

claim: The twelve games were Table Tennis, Tennis, Hockey, Football, Ski, Submarine, Cat and Mouse, Haunted House, Analogic, Roulette, States and Simon Says.
evidence: Ralph H. Baer, Videogames: In the Beginning (Rolenta Press, 2005)
Marty Goldberg, 'Retroinspection: Magnavox Odyssey', in Retro Gamer, Videogames Hardware Handbook volume 1, 2nd edition (Imagine Publishing, 2016), pp. 8–15
qualification: Checked against the Fig. 70 list in Baer. The flier text supports the descriptions of Roulette, States and Simon Says.

claim: Haunted House was a two-player detective-and-ghost game, half on screen and half with clue cards, and the ghost stayed hidden until the right moment.
evidence: Marty Goldberg, 'Retroinspection: Magnavox Odyssey', in Retro Gamer, Videogames Hardware Handbook volume 1, 2nd edition (Imagine Publishing, 2016), pp. 8–15
Ralph H. Baer, Videogames: In the Beginning (Rolenta Press, 2005)
qualification: Agrees with reviewed genres/horror-games.

claim: In Cat and Mouse the maze existed only on the overlay, and players kept to it on their honour.
evidence: Marty Goldberg, 'Retroinspection: Magnavox Odyssey', in Retro Gamer, Videogames Hardware Handbook volume 1, 2nd edition (Imagine Publishing, 2016), pp. 8–15
qualification: The entry attributes this to Retro Gamer.

claim: The only accessory ever released for the accessory port was a pump-action plastic rifle sold separately for $25 for the Shooting Gallery games. It was the first light gun made for a home console.
evidence: Ralph H. Baer, Videogames: In the Beginning (Rolenta Press, 2005)
Marty Goldberg, 'Retroinspection: Magnavox Odyssey', in Retro Gamer, Videogames Hardware Handbook volume 1, 2nd edition (Imagine Publishing, 2016), pp. 8–15
David Winter, 'Magnavox Odyssey', PONG-Story, https://pong-story.com/odyssey.htm
qualification: 'First for a home console' follows from the first-console claim. Agrees with reviewed hardware/light-gun.

claim: Magnavox sold add-on game packs (each with an overlay, instructions and sometimes a new card); Winter counts ten extra games, six from 1972 and four from 1973. Baer said they barely sold, sitting under counters at $5.95, because sales staff were never trained to push them.
evidence: Ralph H. Baer, Videogames: In the Beginning (Rolenta Press, 2005)
Steve Bloom, interview with Ralph Baer, Video Games, vol. 1 no. 5, February 1983, pp. 20–24 and 80–81
David Winter, 'Magnavox Odyssey', PONG-Story, https://pong-story.com/odyssey.htm
qualification: That the packs did not sell is Baer's view and is attributed to him. Baer is internally inconsistent: 'six additional game packs' on one page, and 'ten additional plug-in carts ... in two different game packs' on the next.

claim: The Profit Caravan dealer and press tour began in Phoenix on 3 May 1972; Baer saw the New York presentation on 22 May; Bushnell played the ping-pong game at the Airport Marina, Burlingame, on 24 May. Winter puts the first dealer and press shows in April.
evidence: Ralph H. Baer, Videogames: In the Beginning (Rolenta Press, 2005)
Frank Lovece, 'The Birth of a Notion', Video Games, vol. 2 no. 4, January 1984, pp. 40–43
David Winter, 'Magnavox Odyssey', PONG-Story, https://pong-story.com/odyssey.htm
qualification: Lovece gives Phoenix on 3 May and Burlingame on 23–25 May; Baer gives Burlingame on 24–25 May. Winter places the New York (Bowling Greene) show in April and Burlingame on 24 May. Agrees with games/pong and people/nolan-bushnell.

claim: Production units reached dealers in the months after May 1972; Retro Gamer and Winter give August 1972, while Video Games (1984) says production began on 27 January 1972.
evidence: Ralph H. Baer, Videogames: In the Beginning (Rolenta Press, 2005)
Marty Goldberg, 'Retroinspection: Magnavox Odyssey', in Retro Gamer, Videogames Hardware Handbook volume 1, 2nd edition (Imagine Publishing, 2016), pp. 8–15
David Winter, 'Magnavox Odyssey', PONG-Story, https://pong-story.com/odyssey.htm
Frank Lovece, 'The Birth of a Notion', Video Games, vol. 2 no. 4, January 1984, pp. 40–43
qualification: The year is 1972; the month is disputed, and the entry says so.

claim: Baer said Magnavox restricted sales to its own franchised dealers and that its autumn TV advertising suggested the Odyssey worked only with Magnavox sets ('manifest nonsense').
evidence: Ralph H. Baer, Videogames: In the Beginning (Rolenta Press, 2005)
Steve Bloom, interview with Ralph Baer, Video Games, vol. 1 no. 5, February 1983, pp. 20–24 and 80–81
David Winter, 'Magnavox Odyssey', PONG-Story, https://pong-story.com/odyssey.htm
qualification: Both accounts are Baer's. The book says 'mainly limited', so 'only' was softened. Winter repeats the point but follows Baer's text closely.

claim: A Frank Sinatra TV commercial helped sales in autumn 1972.
evidence: Ralph H. Baer, Videogames: In the Beginning (Rolenta Press, 2005)
David Winter, 'Magnavox Odyssey', PONG-Story, https://pong-story.com/odyssey.htm
qualification: Winter also mentions it, but in wording almost identical to Baer's, so it is not independent. Treat it as Baer's account; the entry attributes it to him.

claim: Close to 100,000 Odysseys were sold in 1972 by Baer's count. Production that year was 140,100 according to Baer, over 130,000 according to Winter and 130,000 according to Retro Gamer.
evidence: Ralph H. Baer, Videogames: In the Beginning (Rolenta Press, 2005)
Steve Bloom, interview with Ralph Baer, Video Games, vol. 1 no. 5, February 1983, pp. 20–24 and 80–81
David Winter, 'Magnavox Odyssey', PONG-Story, https://pong-story.com/odyssey.htm
Marty Goldberg, 'Retroinspection: Magnavox Odyssey', in Retro Gamer, Videogames Hardware Handbook volume 1, 2nd edition (Imagine Publishing, 2016), pp. 8–15
qualification: Located the 140,100 figure. It is in Baer's '1973 – Rethinking My Act' section: 'the 1972 run of 140,100 units'. So genres/horror-games is right to cite it. Baer is internally inconsistent: elsewhere he says 27,000 made in 1973 brought the total to 'about 160,000'. In the interview, the 100,000 figure is the interviewer's.

claim: Baer said Magnavox, having built more than it sold, hardly promoted the Odyssey in 1973, and the price fell to $79: early 1973 according to Baer, late 1973 according to Winter, who also gives a $49.95 price with a new Magnavox TV.
evidence: Ralph H. Baer, Videogames: In the Beginning (Rolenta Press, 2005)
Steve Bloom, interview with Ralph Baer, Video Games, vol. 1 no. 5, February 1983, pp. 20–24 and 80–81
David Winter, 'Magnavox Odyssey', PONG-Story, https://pong-story.com/odyssey.htm
qualification: The interview says 'didn't build, push or advertise at all in '73', but the book says 27,000 more were built in 1973. Winter's page also says discounting had begun 'by early 1973' while dating the $79 price to late 1973. The $49.95 bundle comes from Winter only.

claim: Sales picked up in 1974 with heavy promotion (150,000 units by Baer's account); production of the original ran until 1975, totalling about 350,000 (Baer) or over 330,000 (Winter, Retro Gamer).
evidence: Ralph H. Baer, Videogames: In the Beginning (Rolenta Press, 2005)
Marty Goldberg, 'Retroinspection: Magnavox Odyssey', in Retro Gamer, Videogames Hardware Handbook volume 1, 2nd edition (Imagine Publishing, 2016), pp. 8–15
David Winter, 'Magnavox Odyssey', PONG-Story, https://pong-story.com/odyssey.htm
qualification: The 150,000 figure is Baer's alone. The same book also says the 1974 production run 'topped 170,000'.

claim: Baer estimated the Odyssey made Magnavox little money: production costs of about $40–50 a unit, about $17 million in total costs, about 40,000 returns, and receipts of about $20 million.
evidence: Ralph H. Baer, Videogames: In the Beginning (Rolenta Press, 2005)
qualification: Checked in '1974 – Tracking Magnavox'. These are Baer's own estimates and the entry attributes them to him.

claim: Winter records the first export as the Magnavox Odisea in Mexico from about October 1972, fewer than 4,000 made, with Spanish paperwork.
evidence: David Winter, 'Magnavox Odyssey', PONG-Story, https://pong-story.com/odyssey.htm
qualification: Attributed to Winter in the entry.

claim: In Germany it was sold as the ITT Schaub-Lorenz 'Odyssee' with German manuals, announced in late 1973 and sold in small numbers from early 1974.
evidence: Ralph H. Baer, Videogames: In the Beginning (Rolenta Press, 2005)
David Winter, 'Magnavox Odyssey', PONG-Story, https://pong-story.com/odyssey.htm
qualification: Dates corrected to follow Winter. Baer cites Winter's site for the German manuals, so the two are not independent.

claim: Winter records a Portuguese-language Odyssey sold in Brazil from late 1975 by Planil of Rio de Janeiro under licence.
evidence: David Winter, 'Magnavox Odyssey', PONG-Story, https://pong-story.com/odyssey.htm
qualification: Attributed to Winter. A Brazilian period source would be needed to treat this as settled.

claim: Baer lists twelve countries for the export model (Australia, Belgium, England, France, Germany, Greece, Israel, Italy, Spain, Switzerland, the USSR, Venezuela). The export model dropped Cat and Mouse, Football, Haunted House, Roulette and States, and added Soccer, Volleyball and Wipe Out.
evidence: Ralph H. Baer, Videogames: In the Beginning (Rolenta Press, 2005)
David Winter, 'Magnavox Odyssey', PONG-Story, https://pong-story.com/odyssey.htm
qualification: Winter's patent label confirms only Greece and Israel. The full country list is Baer's.

claim: Sweden's Kanal 34 bore little resemblance to the Odyssey outside but used the same circuits (Baer); Winter dates it to 1975. Baer called Britain's Videomaster Home T.V. Game (early 1974) the first original design after the Odyssey.
evidence: Ralph H. Baer, Videogames: In the Beginning (Rolenta Press, 2005)
David Winter, 'Magnavox Odyssey', PONG-Story, https://pong-story.com/odyssey.htm
qualification: The Videomaster claim is Baer's alone and is attributed to him.

claim: Atari's arcade Pong of autumn 1972 was, in Baer's words, 'a derivative of Odyssey'.
evidence: Steve Bloom, interview with Ralph Baer, Video Games, vol. 1 no. 5, February 1983, pp. 20–24 and 80–81
Frank Lovece, 'The Birth of a Notion', Video Games, vol. 2 no. 4, January 1984, pp. 40–43
Ralph H. Baer, Videogames: In the Beginning (Rolenta Press, 2005)
qualification: Kept to two sentences, linking to reviewed games/pong.

claim: In 1975 Magnavox replaced the original with the Odyssey 100 and 200, built on Texas Instruments chips, while Atari sold home Pong through Sears.
evidence: Ralph H. Baer, Videogames: In the Beginning (Rolenta Press, 2005)
Marty Goldberg, 'Retroinspection: Magnavox Odyssey', in Retro Gamer, Videogames Hardware Handbook volume 1, 2nd edition (Imagine Publishing, 2016), pp. 8–15
David Winter, 'Magnavox Odyssey', PONG-Story, https://pong-story.com/odyssey.htm
qualification: Video Games (1983, 1984) misnamed the 1972 machine the 'Odyssey 100'; the entry says the original was sold simply as the Odyssey.

claim: Magnavox then belonged to Philips, which sold the Odyssey 200 in Britain in 1976. The name passed to the 1978 Odyssey², sold by Philips as the Videopac G7000.
evidence: Marty Goldberg, 'Retroinspection: Magnavox Odyssey', in Retro Gamer, Videogames Hardware Handbook volume 1, 2nd edition (Imagine Publishing, 2016), pp. 8–15
Ralph H. Baer, Videogames: In the Beginning (Rolenta Press, 2005)
qualification: The 1978 date and the G7000 name come from Retro Gamer only. Baer's 1977 log entry confirms the Odyssey 2 plan and a PAL Philips version, but not the year of release. The year of the Philips takeover is left unstated.

claim: Electronic Games credited Magnavox veteran Steve Laner with designing the Odyssey's overlays.
evidence: Electronic Games, vol. 1 no. 2, March 1982, p. 8 (feature on Odyssey² designers)
qualification: Checked: 'this company veteran designed the plastic screen overlays for the original Odyssey'. Attributed to Electronic Games.

claim: The VRC6 is a Konami cartridge chip for the Famicom. It switches memory banks and adds three sound channels, two pulse waves and one sawtooth, to the console's own five.
evidence: Kevin Horton, "VRCVI Chip Info", The RENES Project, v1.01, 31 August 1999, https://www.nesdev.org/vrcvi.txt
NESdev Wiki, "VRC6 audio", https://www.nesdev.org/wiki/VRC6_audio
Morito Shigihara (鴫原盛之), Music from Konami Antiques: Family Computer listening report, GAME Watch, 15 November 2023, https://game.watch.impress.co.jp/docs/kikaku/1546206-3.html
qualification: Checked: Horton and NESdev give the channels; GAME Watch p.3 says '矩形波2音+ノコギリ波1音'.

claim: Only three commercial games used it: Akumajō Densetsu, Mōryō Senki MADARA and Esper Dream 2.
evidence: NESdev Wiki, "List of mappers by release date" and "List of games with expansion audio", https://www.nesdev.org/wiki/List_of_games_with_expansion_audio
NESdev Wiki, "VRC6", https://www.nesdev.org/wiki/VRC6
Morito Shigihara (鴫原盛之), Music from Konami Antiques: Family Computer listening report, GAME Watch, 15 November 2023, https://game.watch.impress.co.jp/docs/kikaku/1546206-3.html
qualification: Checked GAME Watch: page 3 names Akumajō Densetsu and MADARA, and page 4 (DISC13) names Esper Dream 2, but it does not claim the list is complete. The completeness comes from NESdev ('the three commercial VRC6 games'). The entry no longer gives an order for MADARA and Esper Dream 2.

claim: The first VRC6 cartridge, Akumajō Densetsu, came out in Japan on 22 December 1989 (introduced: 1989).
evidence: John Szczepaniak, "The Making of: Super Castlevania IV", Retro Gamer issue 119, Imagine Publishing, 2013, pp. 30-31
NESdev Wiki, "List of mappers by release date" and "List of games with expansion audio", https://www.nesdev.org/wiki/List_of_games_with_expansion_audio
qualification: NESdev lists mapper 24 'Konami VRC6' at 1989-12-22 with Akumajou Densetsu. The article text reads 'CVIII was released in Japan on 22 December 1989'.

claim: Akumajō Densetsu was the first game to use the chip. A 2015 Famitsu.com report names MADARA as Konami's first expansion-audio game, which conflicts with this.
evidence: NESdev Wiki, "List of mappers by release date" and "List of games with expansion audio", https://www.nesdev.org/wiki/List_of_games_with_expansion_audio
Jeremy Parish, "An interview with Konami's Hidenori Maezawa, pt. 2", Retronauts blog, 1UP.com, 14 January 2009 (archived)
Morito Shigihara (鴫原盛之), Music from Konami Antiques: Family Computer listening report, GAME Watch, 15 November 2023, https://game.watch.impress.co.jp/docs/kikaku/1546206-3.html
Famitsu.com, MADARA series soundtrack reissue report, 13 November 2015, https://www.famitsu.com/news/201511/13092957.html
qualification: Presented as a documented disagreement. Quotes checked against both Japanese pages. MADARA's release date is unsourced, so the draft's 'MADARA came out in 1990' was removed. Maezawa only says 'I think'.

claim: Hidenori Maezawa, a Konami composer and sound programmer, told 1UP.com's Jeremy Parish in 2009 that he was involved in designing the VRC6. In his words, 'other technical people … put the parts together', and he thought the chip was first used in Akumajou Densetsu. He did not work on the US port, so he did not have to tone down the music for the NES himself.
evidence: Jeremy Parish, "An interview with Konami's Hidenori Maezawa, pt. 2", Retronauts blog, 1UP.com, 14 January 2009 (archived)
qualification: Checked against the archived post. 1UP introduces him as 'former Konami composer and audio programmer', and the quotes are verbatim. It is attributed recollection and not independently corroborated. His waveform description is not repeated.

claim: Each pulse channel has a 4-bit volume and a 3-bit duty setting in sixteenths, from 1/16 (6.25%) to 8/16 (50%). A mode bit ('digitized' in Horton's terms) ignores the duty and outputs the volume as a steady level. The 2A03's pulses have four duty settings.
evidence: Kevin Horton, "VRCVI Chip Info", The RENES Project, v1.01, 31 August 1999, https://www.nesdev.org/vrcvi.txt
NESdev Wiki, "VRC6 audio", https://www.nesdev.org/wiki/VRC6_audio
qualification: The 2A03 comparison comes from the reviewed hardware/apu entry.

claim: The sawtooth comes from an 8-bit accumulator. A rate value is added on each step and the top 5 bits are output. After six additions the accumulator resets to zero. Rates above 42 wrap and distort. In NESdev's account the divide-by-14 comes from seven steps of two timer ticks each.
evidence: Kevin Horton, "VRCVI Chip Info", The RENES Project, v1.01, 31 August 1999, https://www.nesdev.org/vrcvi.txt
NESdev Wiki, "VRC6 audio", https://www.nesdev.org/wiki/VRC6_audio
qualification: The 42 limit and the every-second-clock detail come from NESdev alone. Horton says only that oversized values (e.g. 30h) wrap.

claim: Pitch comes from 12-bit period registers clocked by the CPU's 1.79 MHz. Pulse frequency is CPU/(16(t+1)) and sawtooth frequency is CPU/(14(t+1)).
evidence: Kevin Horton, "VRCVI Chip Info", The RENES Project, v1.01, 31 August 1999, https://www.nesdev.org/vrcvi.txt
NESdev Wiki, "VRC6 audio", https://www.nesdev.org/wiki/VRC6_audio
qualification: The comparison with the 2A03's 11-bit period comes from the reviewed hardware/apu entry.

claim: The three channels are summed into a 6-bit value on six output pins. That value drives an R-2R resistor-ladder DAC on the cartridge, and the result is mixed with the 2A03's sound.
evidence: Kevin Horton, "VRCVI Chip Info", The RENES Project, v1.01, 31 August 1999, https://www.nesdev.org/vrcvi.txt
NESdev Wiki, "VRC6 pinout", https://www.nesdev.org/wiki/VRC6_pinout
NESdev Wiki, "VRC6 audio", https://www.nesdev.org/wiki/VRC6_audio
qualification: Horton and NESdev agree.

claim: A $9003 register can halt all the oscillators or raise all their frequencies 16 or 256 times. All three games write $00 to it.
evidence: NESdev Wiki, "VRC6 audio", https://www.nesdev.org/wiki/VRC6_audio
qualification: Horton's document does not describe this register, and his register numbering is offset. The entry attributes the claim to NESdev.

claim: The VRC6 pulse channels are inverted in polarity compared with the 2A03's, and the VRC6's DAC appears linear where the 2A03's is not.
evidence: NESdev Wiki, "VRC6 audio", https://www.nesdev.org/wiki/VRC6_audio
qualification: Attributed to NESdev in the prose.

claim: The Famicom routes its own sound out through the cartridge (pin 45, already amplified) and back to the RF output (pin 46), so a cartridge can mix in its own sound. The NES's 72-pin slot has no such path, so the VRC6 is a Famicom-only chip, and an NES has to be modified to hear cartridge audio.
evidence: NESdev Wiki, "Cartridge connector", https://www.nesdev.org/wiki/Cartridge_connector
Kevin Horton, "VRCVI Chip Info", The RENES Project, v1.01, 31 August 1999, https://www.nesdev.org/vrcvi.txt
Firebug, "Comprehensive NES Mapper Document" v0.80 (dated 1997-98 in the document; distributed in mappers.zip), https://www.nesdev.org/mappers.zip
qualification: Agrees with the reviewed APU, cartridge, MMC5 and NES entries. Firebug's wording is hedged ('As far as I know'). The EXP6 convention comes from NESdev only.

claim: The Western Castlevania III was rebuilt on Nintendo's MMC5 and plays its music through the 2A03 alone.
evidence: NESdev Wiki, "VRC6", https://www.nesdev.org/wiki/VRC6
Jeremy Parish, "An interview with Konami's Hidenori Maezawa, pt. 2", Retronauts blog, 1UP.com, 14 January 2009 (archived)
qualification: Established in the reviewed hardware/mmc5, hardware/apu and games/castlevania entries, which cite Nintendo Power. The NESdev VRC6 page itself does not mention the MMC5. The 1UP interviewer says only that the US version 'didn't have the same chip'.

claim: On the mapper side, a 16 KB program bank switches at $8000 and an 8 KB bank at $C000. The top 8 KB is fixed, and there are eight 1 KB graphics banks.
evidence: NESdev Wiki, "VRC6", https://www.nesdev.org/wiki/VRC6
Firebug, "Comprehensive NES Mapper Document" v0.80 (dated 1997-98 in the document; distributed in mappers.zip), https://www.nesdev.org/mappers.zip
qualification: Firebug confirms 'The last 8K of ROM is permanently hard-wired'.

claim: It has an IRQ counter, the design it shares with the VRC4 and VRC7, that counts either CPU cycles or scanlines measured in CPU cycles.
evidence: NESdev Wiki, "VRC6", https://www.nesdev.org/wiki/VRC6
Firebug, "Comprehensive NES Mapper Document" v0.80 (dated 1997-98 in the document; distributed in mappers.zip), https://www.nesdev.org/mappers.zip
qualification: Firebug documents the $F000-$F002 registers and a counter running every 113.75 cycles. The cycle/scanline mode and the shared VRC IRQ design come from NESdev ('VRC6' and 'VRC IRQ').

claim: There are two board wirings: VRC6a (Akumajō Densetsu, iNES mapper 24, board 351951) and VRC6b (MADARA and Esper Dream 2, mapper 26, board 351949A). They have CPU address lines A0 and A1 swapped, so $x001 and $x002 trade places.
evidence: NESdev Wiki, "VRC6", https://www.nesdev.org/wiki/VRC6
NESdev Wiki, "NSF", https://www.nesdev.org/wiki/NSF
NESdev Wiki, "VRC6 pinout", https://www.nesdev.org/wiki/VRC6_pinout
qualification: All three are NESdev pages. Horton independently notes that A0/A1 'are reversed' on some carts. The VRC2 entry explains that mapper numbers are an emulator convention.

claim: The chip supports nametables from cartridge ROM and a larger-CHR board that Konami never built. The three games did not use ROM nametables.
evidence: NESdev Wiki, "VRC6", https://www.nesdev.org/wiki/VRC6
qualification: NESdev: 'intended for a different PCB (never used)', and 'the three commercial VRC6 games neither provided extra nametable RAM, nor used ROM nametables'.

claim: It is a 48-pin DIP. Known parts are marked 053328, 053329 and 053330 'VRC VI', and the 053330 die is an S-MOS SLA7340 gate array.
evidence: NESdev Wiki, "VRC6 pinout", https://www.nesdev.org/wiki/VRC6_pinout
Kevin Horton, "VRCVI Chip Info", The RENES Project, v1.01, 31 August 1999, https://www.nesdev.org/vrcvi.txt
qualification: Horton confirms only the 48-pin, 600-mil DIP. The part numbers, the three revisions and the die marking come from NESdev alone, and the prose says so.

claim: The NSF music format has a header flag for VRC6 audio (byte $07B, bit 0). FamiTracker added VRC6 support in version 0.2.9 (January 2009).
evidence: NESdev Wiki, "NSF", https://www.nesdev.org/wiki/NSF
FamiTracker 0.4.6 help file and source code, 2015 (as cited by the reviewed software/famitracker entry)
qualification: These are two separate facts, each with one source. The FamiTracker date is taken from the reviewed famitracker entry and was not rechecked here.

claim: Shovel Knight (2014) let its NES-style score use the VRC6's three extra channels, and Jake Kaufman wrote the main score in FamiTracker.
evidence: David D'Angelo, "Breaking the NES for Shovel Knight", Gamasutra, 25 June 2014, https://www.gamedeveloper.com/design/breaking-the-nes-for-shovel-knight
qualification: The wording matches the reviewed games/shovel-knight entry, and the entry links to it.

claim: Masahiro Ueno, a Konami programmer, recalled in Retro Gamer in 2013 that Konami 'had the best sound team'. Of his team's move to the Super Famicom, he said 'we felt we'd done everything we could do on the Famicom without additional chips in the cartridge'.
evidence: John Szczepaniak, "The Making of: Super Castlevania IV", Retro Gamer issue 119, Imagine Publishing, 2013, pp. 30-31
qualification: Corrected. The second quote is about the move to the Super Famicom, not about the Famicom Castlevania III team. It is an attributed retrospective quote, used only as colour.
